messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane, a 63‑year‑old community organizer of Māori descent, lives in a modest house on the outskirts of a suburban town. He has spent the past decade rallying residents to fight for better housing and environmental justice, but an accident three years ago has left him trapped in a quiet house, his movements limited by a fractured leg and a mind that refuses to stay still. The day he was hit by a drunk driver while heading home from a meeting, the world collapsed in a sudden burst of light and heat. He remembers the scream of the tires on wet asphalt, the metallic clang of the steering wheel, and the flash of the driver’s angry face, but many details are shrouded in blackness; the event is a patchwork of sharp clarity and total blankness. When he attempts to recount it, words elude him, and he feels an emptiness that feels like a dead inside. The first time Tane heard another person speak angrily—at a council meeting where residents argued over a new development—he felt his heart pound and a phantom sting of violence surge through his body. That simple, calm expression of anger activated his belief that the world is hostile, and he began to think that he had somehow deserved the trauma. He started to blame himself for not seeing the drunk driver, for not staying on a different street, for not being able to protect himself. The anger in others, even when not loud, felt like a reminder that his actions had contributed to the danger, and it amplified his sense that the world remained unsafe. This chain of thought hardened his emotional numbness, as he found it increasingly hard to feel relief or joy after the incident. Because he constantly blamed himself, Tane’s mind struggled to stitch together the fragments of that day. The self‑blame made him focus on every gap, every blank, as evidence of his failure. He could not find words to explain the crash; the memory of the collision became a source of humiliation. He told himself that the incompleteness of his recollection meant he had been negligent. The lack of a full narrative left him feeling more dead inside, as though his life had stopped at the point of the accident. The sharper memories of the screeching tires seemed to haunt him, while the missing parts left a void that he could not fill, reinforcing his belief that he had caused the tragedy. The ongoing belief that he had caused the accident made Tane hypervigilant for any sign of danger, especially when others showed anger or wore police or military uniforms that reminded him of the emergency response he had received at the scene. He began to see uniforms as symbols of threat, a reminder that help could be both a blessing and a reminder of the violence that had struck him. This perception caused him to withdraw from many community gatherings where heated debate was inevitable or where police presence was expected. He would skip volunteer work, turn down invitations, and choose solitude over the loud discussions that might ignite his body’s reaction to danger. He had come to believe that avoiding such environments would protect him from the pain of reliving the accident. The memory gaps that plagued him also made him wary of situations that could trigger the same sense of loss and fear. Whenever he recalled an event where someone’s uniform was present—a traffic stop at a festival or a protest in front of a police station—he felt the old jolt of panic that had rushed through him at the time of the crash. These flashbacks were brief, often just a flicker of the uniform’s silhouette or the echo of a command shouted in a thick accent. The images, even when only half-remembered, were enough to provoke the same bodily threat response, reinforcing his belief that the world remained a dangerous place. Now, Tane sits on the porch of his house, watching the neighbor’s children play, his mind drifting to the day when his life shifted. He has decided to seek help because each avoidance leaves him feeling more isolated from the community he loves. He fears that he will never be able to speak at a rally again without feeling as if a gunshot is waiting in the crowd. Yet he also hopes that, with professional guidance, he can untangle the knots between his memory, his anger‑triggered appraisals, and the bodily sensations that bind them, allowing him to rejoin the community he has always served.
